entries.25086a909a5738f05af57a82cd725371f5094e32: <div sID="gen14930" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Eccl.5" sID="Eccl.5"/> <div eID="gen14930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14931" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14932" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in this chapter, discourses, I. Concerning the worship of God, prescribing that as a remedy against all those vanities which he had already observed to be in wisdom, learning, pleasure, honour, power, and business. That we may not be deceived by those things, nor have our spirits vexed with the disappointments we meet with in them, let us make conscience of our duty to God and keep up our communion with him; but, withal, he gives a necessary caution against the vanities which are too often found in religious exercises, which deprive them of their excellency and render them unable to help against other vanities. If our religion be a vain religion, how great is that vanity! Let us therefore take heed of vanity, 1. In hearing the word, and offering sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">ver. 1</reference>. 2. In prayer, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2-Eccl.5.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. 3. In making vows, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. 4. In pretending to divine dreams, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">ver. 7</reference>. Now, (1.) For a remedy against those vanities, he prescribes the fear of God, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">ver. 7</reference>. (2.) To prevent the offence that might arise from the present sufferings of good people, he directs us to look up to God, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">ver. 8</reference>. II. Concerning the wealth of this world and the vanity and vexation that attend it. The fruits of the earth indeed are necessary to the support of life (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.9">ver. 9</reference>), but as for silver, and gold, and riches, 1. They are unsatisfying, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">ver. 10</reference>. 2. They are unprofitable, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">ver. 11</reference>. 3. They are disquieting, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">ver. 12</reference>. 4. They often prove hurtful and destroying, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.13">ver. 13</reference>. 5. They are perishing, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.14">ver. 14</reference>. 6. They must be left behind when we die, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.15-Eccl.5.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. 7. If we have not a heart to make use of them, they occasion a great deal of uneasiness, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">ver. 17</reference>. And therefore he recommends to us the comfortable use of that which God has given us, with an eye to him that is the giver, as the best way both to answer the end of our having it and to obviate the mischiefs that commonly attend great estates, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18-Eccl.5.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. So that if we can but learn out of this chapter how to manage the business of religion, and the business of this world (which two take up most of our time), so that both may turn to a good account, and neither our sabbath days nor our week-days may be lost, we shall have reason to say, We have learned two good lessons.
entries.332412490bc66db3a890c45a4e6cc4b20bc8762a: <div eID="gen14932" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14931" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Caution to Worshippers.</title> <div sID="gen14933" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil. <hi type="super">2</hi> Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing before God: for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few. <hi type="super">3</hi> For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice <hi type="italic">is known</hi> by multitude of words. <div eID="gen14933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14934" type="x-p"/> Solomon's design, in driving us off from the world, by showing us its vanity, is to drive us to God and to our duty, that we may not walk in the way of the world, but by religious rules, nor depend upon the wealth of the world, but on religious advantages; and therefore, <div eID="gen14934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14935" type="x-p"/> I. He here sends us to <hi type="italic">the house of God,</hi> to the place of public worship, to the temple, which he himself had built at a vast expense. When he reflected with regret on all his other works (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.4">ch. ii. 4</reference>), he did not repent of that, but reflected on it with pleasure, yet mentions it not, lest he should seem to reflect on it with pride; but he here sends those to it that would know more of the vanity of the world and would find that happiness which is in vain sought for in the creature. David, when he was perplexed, <hi type="italic">went into the sanctuary of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>. Let our disappointments in the creature turn our eyes to the Creator; let us have recourse to the word of God's grace and consult that, to the throne of his grace and solicit that. In the word and prayer there is a balm for every wound. <div eID="gen14935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14936" type="x-p"/> II. He charges us to behave ourselves well there, that we may not miss of our end in coming thither. Religious exercises are not vain things, but, if we mismanage them, they become vain to us. And therefore, <div eID="gen14936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14937" type="x-p"/> 1. We must address ourselves to them with all possible seriousness and care: "<hi type="italic">Keep thy foot,</hi> not keep it back from the house of God (as <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Prov. xxv. 17</reference>), nor go slowly thither, as one unwilling to draw nigh to God, but <hi type="italic">look well to thy goings, ponder the path of thy feet,</hi> lest thou take a false step. Address thyself to the worship of God with a solemn pause, and take time to compose thyself for it, not going about it with precipitation, which is called <hi type="italic">hasting with the feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.19.2">Prov. xix. 2</reference>. Keep thy thoughts from roving and wandering from the work; keep thy affections from running out towards wrong objects, for in the business of God's house there is work enough for the whole man, and all too little to be employed." Some think it alludes to the charge given to Moses and Joshua to <hi type="italic">put off their shoes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Exod. iii. 5,</reference> <reference osisRef="Josh.5.15">Josh. v. 15,</reference>) in token of subjection and reverence. <hi type="italic">Keep thy feet</hi> clean, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.19">Exod. xxx. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen14937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> 2. We must take heed that the sacrifice we bring be not <hi type="italic">the sacrifice of fools</hi> (of wicked men), for they are fools and their <hi type="italic">sacrifice is an abomination to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>), that we bring not <hi type="italic">the torn, and the lame, and the sick for sacrifice,</hi> for we are plainly told that it will not be accepted, and therefore it is folly to bring it,—that we rest not in the sign and ceremony, and the outside of the performance, without regarding the sense and meaning of it, for that is the <hi type="italic">sacrifice of fools.</hi> Bodily exercise, if that be all, is a jest; none but fools will think thus to please him who is a Spirit and requires the heart, and they will see their folly when they find what a great deal of pains they have taken to no purpose for want of sincerity. They are <hi type="italic">fools,</hi> for they <hi type="italic">consider not that they do evil;</hi> they think they are doing God and themselves good service when really they are putting a great affront upon God and a great cheat upon their own souls by their hypocritical devotions. Men may be doing evil even when they profess to be doing good, and even when they do not know it, when they do not consider it. <hi type="italic">They know not but to do evil,</hi> so some read it. Wicked minds cannot choose but sin, even in the acts of devotion. Or, They <hi type="italic">consider not that they do evil;</hi> they act at a venture, right or wrong, pleasing to God or not, it is all one to them. <div eID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14939" type="x-p"/> 3. That we may not bring <hi type="italic">the sacrifice of fools,</hi> we must come to God's house with hearts disposed to know and do our duty. We must be <hi type="italic">ready to hear,</hi> that is, (1.) We must diligently <hi type="italic">attend</hi> to the word of God read and preached. "<hi type="italic">Be swift to hear</hi> the exposition which the priests give of the sacrifices, declaring the intent and meaning of them, and do not think it enough to gaze upon what they do, for it must be <hi type="italic">a reasonable service,</hi> otherwise it is <hi type="italic">the sacrifice of fools.</hi>" (2.) We must resolve to comply with the will of God as it is made known to us. <hi type="italic">Hearing</hi> is often put for <hi type="italic">obeying,</hi> and that is it that is <hi type="italic">better than sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1 Sam. xv. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15-Isa.1.16">Isa. i. 15, 16</reference>. We come in a right frame to holy duties when we come with this upon our heart, <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears. Let the word of the Lord come</hi> (said a good man), <hi type="italic">and if I had 600 necks I would bow them all to the authority of it.</hi> <div eID="gen14939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14940" type="x-p"/> 4. We must be very cautious and considerate in all our approaches and addresses to God (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be not rash with thy mouth,</hi> in making prayers, or protestations, or promises; <hi type="italic">let not thy heart be hasty to utter any thing before God.</hi> Note, (1.) When we are in the <hi type="italic">house of God,</hi> in solemn assemblies for religious worship, we are in a special manner before God and in his presence, there where he has promised to meet his people, where his eye is upon us and ours ought to be unto him. (2.) We have something to say, something to utter before God, when we <hi type="italic">draw nigh to him</hi> in holy duties; he is one <hi type="italic">with whom we have to do,</hi> with whom we have business of vast importance. If we come without an errand, we shall go away without any advantage. (3.) What we <hi type="italic">utter before God</hi> must come from <hi type="italic">the heart,</hi> and therefore we must not be <hi type="italic">rash with our mouth,</hi> never let our tongue outrun our thoughts in our devotions; the <hi type="italic">words of our mouth,</hi> must always be the product of the <hi type="italic">meditation of our hearts.</hi> Thoughts are words to God, and words are but wind if they be not copied from the thoughts. Lip-labour, though ever so well laboured, if that be all, is but lost labour in religion, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.8-Matt.15.9">Matt. xv. 8, 9</reference>. (4.) It is not enough that what we say comes from the heart, but it must come from a composed heart, and not from a sudden heat or passion. As the mouth must not be rash, so the heart must not be hasty; we must not only think, but think twice, before we speak, when we are to speak either from God in preaching or to God in prayer, and not utter any thing indecent and undigested, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">1 Cor. xiv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen14940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14941" type="x-p"/> 5. We must be sparing of our words in the presence of God, that is, we must be reverent and deliberate, not talk to God as boldly and carelessly as we do to one another, not speak what comes uppermost, not repeat things over and over, as we do to one another, that what we say may be understood and remembered and may make impression; no, when we speak to God we must consider, (1.) That between him and us there is an infinite distance: <hi type="italic">God is in heaven,</hi> where he reigns in glory over us and all the children of men, where he is attended with an innumerable company of holy angels and is <hi type="italic">far exalted above all our blessing and praise. We are on earth,</hi> the footstool of his throne; we are mean and vile, unlike God, and utterly unworthy to receive any favour from him or to have any communion with him. Therefore we must be very grave, humble, and serious, and be reverent in speaking to him, as we are when we speak to a great man that is much our superior; and, in token of this, <hi type="italic">let our words be few,</hi> that they may be <hi type="italic">well chosen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.14">Job ix. 14</reference>. This does not condemn all long prayers; were they not good, the Pharisees would not have used them for a pretence; Christ prayed all night; and we are directed to <hi type="italic">continue in prayer.</hi> But it condemns careless heartless praying, <hi type="italic">vain repetitions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.7">Matt. vi. 7</reference>), repeating <hi type="italic">Pater-nosters</hi> by tale. Let us speak to God, and of him, in his own words, words which the scripture teaches; and let our words, words of our own invention, be few, lest, not speaking by rule, we speak amiss. (2.) That the multiplying of words in our devotions will make them <hi type="italic">the sacrifices of fools,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">v. 3</reference>. As confused dreams, frightful and perplexed, and such as disturb the sleep, are an evidence of a hurry of business which fills our head, so many words and hasty ones, used in prayer, are an evidence of folly reigning in the heart, ignorance of and unacquaintedness with both God and ourselves, low thoughts of God, and careless thoughts of our own souls. Even in common conversation <hi type="italic">a fool is known by the multitude of words;</hi> those that know least talk most (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">ch. x. 11</reference>), particularly in devotion; there, no doubt, <hi type="italic">a prating fool shall fall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">Prov. x. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.10">10</reference>), shall fall short of acceptance. Those are fools indeed who think they <hi type="italic">shall be heard,</hi> in prayer, <hi type="italic">for their much speaking.</hi>
entries.f4e6886c9f8f9700f49b2bfdbf3ac2e19b9d7dd6: <div eID="gen14941" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Obligation of a Vow.</title> <div sID="gen14942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for <hi type="italic">he hath</hi> no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. <hi type="super">5</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is it</hi> that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. <hi type="super">6</hi> Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it <hi type="italic">was</hi> an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands? <hi type="super">7</hi> For in the multitude of dreams and many words <hi type="italic">there are</hi> also <hi type="italic">divers</hi> vanities: but fear thou God. <hi type="super">8</hi> If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> higher than the highest regardeth; and <hi type="italic">there be</hi> higher than they. <div eID="gen14942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14943" type="x-p"/> Four things we are exhorted to in these verses:— <div eID="gen14943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14944" type="x-p"/> I. To be conscientious in paying our vows. <div eID="gen14944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14945" type="x-p"/> 1. A vow is a bond upon the soul (<reference osisRef="Num.30.2">Num. xxx. 2</reference>), by which we solemnly oblige ourselves, not only, in general, to do that which we are already bound to do, but, in some particular instances, to do that to do which we were not under any antecedent obligation, whether it respects honouring God or serving the interests of his kingdom among men. When, under the sense of some affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.14">Ps. lxvi. 14</reference>), or in the pursuit of some mercy (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.11">1 Sam. i. 11</reference>), thou hast vowed such a vow as this <hi type="italic">unto God,</hi> know that <hi type="italic">thou hast opened thy mouth unto the Lord and thou canst not go back;</hi> therefore, (1.) Pay it; perform what thou hast promised; bring to God what thou hast dedicated and devoted to him: <hi type="italic">Pay that which thou hast vowed;</hi> pay it in full and <hi type="italic">keep not back any part of the price;</hi> pay it in kind, do not <hi type="italic">alter it or change it,</hi> so the law was, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.10">Lev. xxvii. 10</reference>. Have we vowed to <hi type="italic">give our own selves unto the Lord?</hi> Let us then be as good as our word, act in his service, to his glory, and not sacrilegiously alienate ourselves. (2.) <hi type="italic">Defer not to pay it.</hi> If it be in the power of thy hands to pay it to-day, leave it not till to-morrow; do not <hi type="italic">beg a day,</hi> nor put it off to a more convenient season. By delay the sense of the obligation slackens and cools, and is in danger of wearing off; we thereby discover a loathness and backwardness to perform our vow; and <hi type="italic">qui non est hodie cras minus aptus erit—he who is not inclined to-day will be averse to-morrow.</hi> The longer it is put off the more difficult it will be to bring ourselves to it; death may not only prevent the payment, but fetch thee to judgment, under the guilt of a broken vow, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.11">Ps. lxxvi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen14945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14946" type="x-p"/> 2. Two reasons are here given why we should speedily and cheerfully pay our vows:—(1.) Because otherwise we affront God; we play the fool with him, as if we designed to put a trick upon him; and <hi type="italic">God has no pleasure in fools.</hi> More is implied than is expressed; the meaning is, He greatly abhors such fools and such foolish dealings. <hi type="italic">Has he need of fools?</hi> No; <hi type="italic">Be not deceived, God is not mocked,</hi> but will surely and severely reckon with those that thus play fast and loose with him. (2.) Because otherwise we wrong ourselves, we lose the benefit of the making of the <hi type="italic">vow,</hi> nay, we incur the penalty for the breach of it; so that it would have been better a great deal <hi type="italic">not to have vowed,</hi> more safe and more to our advantage, than to <hi type="italic">vow and not to pay.</hi> Not to have <hi type="italic">vowed</hi> would have been but an omission, but to <hi type="italic">vow and not pay</hi> incurs the guilt of treachery and perjury; it is <hi type="italic">lying to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">Acts v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen14946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14947" type="x-p"/> II. To be cautious in making our vows. This is necessary in order to our being conscientious in performing them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">v. 6</reference>. 1. We must take heed that we never vow anything that is sinful, or that may be an occasion of sin, for such a vow is ill-made and must be broken. <hi type="italic">Suffer not thy mouth,</hi> by such a vow, <hi type="italic">to cause thy flesh to sin,</hi> as Herod's rash promise caused him to cut off the head of John the Baptist. 2. We must not vow that which, through the frailty of the flesh, we have reason to fear we shall not be able to perform, as those that vow a single life and yet know not how to keep their vow. Hereby, (1.) They shame themselves; for they are forced to <hi type="italic">say before the angel, It was an error,</hi> that either they did not mean or did not consider what they said; and, take it which way you will, it is bad enough. "When thou hast made a <hi type="italic">vow,</hi> do not seek to evade it, nor find excuses to get clear of the obligation of it; <hi type="italic">say not before the priest,</hi> who is called the <hi type="italic">angel or messenger of the Lord of hosts,</hi> that, upon second thoughts, thou hast changed thy mind, and desirest to be absolved from the obligation of thy vow; but stick to it, and do not seek a hole to creep out at." Some by <hi type="italic">the angel</hi> understand the guardian angel which they suppose to attend every man and to inspect what he does. Others understand it of Christ, <hi type="italic">the Angel of the covenant,</hi> who is present with his people in their assemblies, who searches the heart, and cannot be imposed upon; <hi type="italic">provoke him not, for God's name is in him,</hi> and he is represented as strict and jealous, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.20-Exod.23.21">Exod. xxiii. 20, 21</reference>. (2.) They expose themselves to the wrath of God, for he is <hi type="italic">angry at the voice of</hi> those that thus <hi type="italic">lie unto him with their mouth and flatter him with their tongue,</hi> and is displeased at their dissimulation, and <hi type="italic">destroys the works of their hands,</hi> that is, blasts their enterprises, and defeats those purposes which, when they made these vows, they were seeking to God for the success of. If we treacherously cancel the words of our mouths, and revoke our vows, God will justly overthrow our projects, and walk contrary, and at all adventures, with those that thus walk contrary, and at all adventures with him. It is <hi type="italic">a snare to a man, after vows, to make enquiry.</hi> <div eID="gen14947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14948" type="x-p"/> III. To keep up the fear of God, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Many, of old, pretended to know the mind of God by <hi type="italic">dreams,</hi> and were so full of them that they almost made God's people forget his name by their <hi type="italic">dreams</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.25-Jer.23.26">Jer. xxiii. 25, 26</reference>); and many now perplex themselves with their frightful or odd dreams, or with other people's dreams, as if they foreboded this or the other disaster. Those that heed dreams shall have a multitude of them to fill their heads with; but in them all <hi type="italic">there are divers vanities,</hi> as there are in many words, and the more if we regard them. "They are but like the idle impertinent chat of children and fools, and therefore never heed them; forget them; instead of repeating them lay no stress upon them, draw no disquieting conclusions from them, but <hi type="italic">fear thou God;</hi> have an eye to his sovereign dominion, set him before thee, keep thyself in his love, and be afraid of offending him, and then thou wilt not disturb thyself with foolish dreams." The way not to be dismayed at the signs of heaven, nor afraid <hi type="italic">of the idols of the heathen,</hi> is to <hi type="italic">fear God as King of nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.2">Jer. x. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen14948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14949" type="x-p"/> IV. With that to keep down the fear of man, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">v. 8</reference>. "Set God before thee, and then, if <hi type="italic">thou seest the oppression of the poor,</hi> thou wilt not <hi type="italic">marvel at the matter,</hi> nor find fault with divine Providence, nor think the worse of the institution of magistracy, when thou seest the ends of it thus perverted, nor of religion, when thou seest it will not secure men from suffering wrong." Observe here, 1. A melancholy sight on earth, and such as cannot but trouble every good man that has a sense of justice and a concern for mankind, to see <hi type="italic">the oppression of the poor</hi> because they are poor and cannot defend themselves, and the <hi type="italic">violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province,</hi> oppression under colour of law and backed with power. The kingdom in general may have a good government, and yet it may so happen that a particular province may be committed to a bad man, by whose mal-administration justice may be perverted; so hard it is for the wisest of kings, in giving preferments, to be sure of their men; they can but redress the grievance when it appears. 2. A comfortable sight in heaven. When things look thus dismal we may satisfy ourselves with this, (1.) That, though oppressors be <hi type="italic">high,</hi> God is <hi type="italic">above them,</hi> and in that very thing wherein <hi type="italic">they deal proudly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">Exod. xviii. 11</reference>. God is <hi type="italic">higher than the highest</hi> of creatures, than the highest of princes, than the king that is <hi type="italic">higher than Agag</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.7">Num. xxiv. 7</reference>), than the highest angels, the <hi type="italic">thrones and dominions</hi> of the upper world. God is the <hi type="italic">Most High over all the earth,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">glory is above the heavens;</hi> before him princes are worms, the brightest but glow-worms. (2.) That, though oppressors be secure, God has his eye upon them, takes notice of, and will reckon for, all their violent perverting of judgment; <hi type="italic">he regards,</hi> not only sees it but observes it, and keeps it on record, to be called over again; his <hi type="italic">eyes are upon their ways.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Job.23.33">Job xxiv. 23</reference>. (3.) That there is a world of angels, for there are <hi type="italic">higher than they,</hi> who are employed by the divine justice for protecting the injured and punishing the injurious. Sennacherib valued himself highly upon his potent army, but one angel proved too hard for him and all his forces. Some, by those <hi type="italic">that are higher than they</hi> understand the great council of the nation, the presidents to whom the <hi type="italic">princes of the provinces are accountable</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">Dan. vi. 2</reference>), the senate that receive complaints against the proconsuls, the courts above to which appeals are made from the inferior courts, which are necessary to the good government of a kingdom. Let it be a check to oppressors that perhaps their superiors on earth may call them to an account; however, God the Supreme in heaven will.
entries.d3c953dd5d34b88ba14214675f8e561e3fa6a122: <div eID="gen14949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vanity of Riches.</title> <div sID="gen14950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king <hi type="italic">himself</hi> is served by the field. <hi type="super">10</hi> He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> also vanity. <hi type="super">11</hi> When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good <hi type="italic">is there</hi> to the owners thereof, saving the beholding <hi type="italic">of them</hi> with their eyes? <hi type="super">12</hi> The sleep of a labouring man <hi type="italic">is</hi> sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. <hi type="super">13</hi> There is a sore evil <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have seen under the sun, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. 14 But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> nothing in his hand. <hi type="super">15</hi> As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand. <hi type="super">16</hi> And this also <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sore evil, <hi type="italic">that</hi> in all points as he came, so shall he go: and what profit hath he that hath laboured for the wind? <hi type="super">17</hi> All his days also he eateth in darkness, and <hi type="italic">he hath</hi> much sorrow and wrath with his sickness. <div eID="gen14950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14951" type="x-p"/> Solomon had shown the vanity of pleasure, gaiety, and fine works, of honour, power, and royal dignity; and there is many a covetous worldling that will agree with him, and speak as slightly as he does of these things; but money, he thinks, is a substantial thing, and if he can but have enough of that he is happy. This is the mistake which Solomon attacks, and attempts to rectify, in these verses; he shows that there is as much vanity in great riches, and the <hi type="italic">lust of the eye</hi> about them, as there is in the <hi type="italic">lusts of the flesh</hi> and the <hi type="italic">pride of life,</hi> and a man can make himself no more happy by hoarding an estate than by spending it. <div eID="gen14951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14952" type="x-p"/> I. He grants that the products of the earth, for the support and comfort of human life, are valuable things (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The profit of the earth is for all.</hi> Man's body, being made of the earth, thence has its maintenance (<reference osisRef="Job.28.5">Job xxviii. 5</reference>); and that it has so, and that a <hi type="italic">barren land</hi> is not <hi type="italic">made his dwelling</hi> (as he has deserved for being rebellious, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.6">Ps. lxviii. 6</reference>), is an instance of God's great bounty to him. There is <hi type="italic">profit to be got out of the earth,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">for all;</hi> all need it; it is appointed for all; there is enough for all. It is not only for all men, but for all the inferior creatures; the same ground brings <hi type="italic">grass for the cattle</hi> that brings <hi type="italic">herbs for the service of men.</hi> Israel had <hi type="italic">bread from heaven, angels' food,</hi> but (which is a humbling consideration) the earth is our storehouse and the beasts are fellow-commoners with us. <hi type="italic">The king himself is served of the field,</hi> and would be ill served, would be quite starved, without its products. This puts a great honour upon the husbandman's calling, that it is the most necessary of all to the support of man's life. The many have the benefit of it; the mighty cannot live without it; it is <hi type="italic">for all;</hi> it is for the <hi type="italic">king himself.</hi> Those that have an abundance of the fruits of the earth must remember <hi type="italic">they are for all,</hi> and therefore must look upon themselves but as stewards of their abundance, out of which they must give to those that need. Dainty meats and soft clothing are only <hi type="italic">for some,</hi> but the <hi type="italic">fruit of the earth is for all.</hi> And even those that <hi type="italic">suck the abundance of the seas</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deut. xxxiii. 19</reference>) cannot be without the fruit of the earth, while those that have a competency of the <hi type="italic">fruit of the earth</hi> may despise the <hi type="italic">abundance of the seas.</hi> <div eID="gen14952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> II. He maintains that the riches that are more than these, that are for hoarding, not for use, are <hi type="italic">vain things,</hi> and will not make a man easy or happy. That which our Saviour has said (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.15">Luke xii. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">that a man's life consists not in the abundance of the things which he possesses,</hi> is what Solomon here undertakes to prove by various arguments. <div eID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14954" type="x-p"/> 1. The more men have the more they would have, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">v. 10</reference>. A man may have but a little silver and be satisfied with it, may know when he has enough and covet no more. <hi type="italic">Godliness, with contentment, is great gain. I have enough,</hi> says Jacob; <hi type="italic">I have all, and abound,</hi> says St. Paul: but, (1.) He that <hi type="italic">loves silver,</hi> and sets his heart upon it, will never think he has enough, but <hi type="italic">enlarges his desire as hell</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab. ii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">lays house to house and field to field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa. v. 8</reference>), and, like <hi type="italic">the daughters of the horse-leech, still cries, Give, give.</hi> Natural desires are at rest when that which is desired is obtained, but corrupt desires are insatiable. Nature is content with little, grace with less, but lust with nothing. (2.) He that has silver in abundance, and has it increasing ever so fast upon him, yet does not find that it yields any solid satisfaction to his soul. There are bodily desires which silver itself will not satisfy; if a man be hungry, ingots of silver will do no more to satisfy his hunger than clods of clay. Much less will worldly abundance satisfy spiritual desires; he that has ever so much silver covets more, not only of that, but of something else, something of another nature. Those that make themselves drudges to the world are spending their <hi type="italic">labour for that which satisfies not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>), which fills the belly, but will never fill the soul, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen14954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> 2. The more men have the more occasion they have for it, and the more they have to do with it, so that it is as broad as it is long: <hi type="italic">When goods increase, they are increased that eat them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">The more meat the more mouths.</hi> Does the estate thrive? And does not the family at the same time grow more numerous and the children grow up to need more? The more men have the better house they must keep, the more servants they must employ, the more guests they must entertain, the more they must give to the poor, and the more they will have hanging on them, for where <hi type="italic">the carcase is the eagles will be.</hi> What we have more than food and raiment we have <hi type="italic">for others;</hi> and then <hi type="italic">what good is there to the owners</hi> themselves, but the pleasure of <hi type="italic">beholding it with their eyes?</hi> And a poor pleasure it is. An empty speculation is all the difference between the owners and the sharers; the owner sees that as his own which those about him enjoy as much of the real benefit of as he; only he has the satisfaction of doing good to others, which indeed is a satisfaction to one who believes what Christ said, that <hi type="italic">it is more blessed to give than to receive;</hi> but to a covetous man, who thinks all lost that goes beside himself, it is a constant vexation to see others eat of his increase. <div eID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14956" type="x-p"/> 3. The more men have the more care they have about it, which perplexes them and disturbs their repose, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">v. 12</reference>. Refreshing sleep is as much the support and comfort of this life as food is. Now, (1.) Those commonly sleep best that work hard and have but what they work for: <hi type="italic">The sleep of the labouring man is sweet,</hi> not only because he has tired himself with his labour, which makes his sleep the more welcome to him and makes him sleep soundly, but because he has little to fill his head with care about and so break his sleep. His sleep is sweet, though he eat but little and have but little to eat, for his weariness rocks him asleep; and, though he eat much, yet he can sleep well, for his labour gets him a good digestion. The sleep of the diligent Christian, and his long sleep, is sweet; for, having spent himself and his time in the service of God, he can cheerfully return to God and repose in him as his rest. (2.) Those that have every thing else often fail to secure a good night's sleep. Either their eyes are held waking or their sleeps are unquiet and do not refresh them; and it is their abundance that breaks their sleep and disturbs it, both the abundance of their care (as the rich man's who, when his ground brought forth plentifully, thought within himself, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.17">Luke xii. 17</reference>) and the abundance of what they eat and drink which overcharges the heart, makes them sick, and so hinders their repose. Ahasuerus, after a banquet of wine, could not sleep; and perhaps consciousness of guilt, both in getting and using what they have, breaks their sleep as much as any thing. But <hi type="italic">God gives his beloved sleep.</hi> <div eID="gen14956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14957" type="x-p"/> 4. The more men have the more danger they are in both of doing mischief and of having mischief done them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is an evil, a sore evil,</hi> which Solomon himself had <hi type="italic">seen under the sun,</hi> in this lower world, this theatre of sin and woe—<hi type="italic">riches left for the owners thereof</hi> (who have been industrious to hoard them and keep them safely) <hi type="italic">to their hurt;</hi> they would have been better without them. (1.) Their riches <hi type="italic">do them hurt,</hi> make them proud, secure, and in love with the world, draw away their hearts from God and duty, and make it very difficult for them to enter into the kingdom of heaven, nay, help to shut them out of it. (2.) They <hi type="italic">do hurt with their riches,</hi> which not only put them into a capacity of gratifying their own lusts and living luxuriously, but give them an opportunity of oppressing others and dealing hardly with them. (3.) Often they sustain <hi type="italic">hurt by their riches.</hi> They would not be envied, would not be robbed, if they were not rich. It is the fat beast that is led first to the slaughter. A very rich man (as one observes) has sometimes been excepted out of a general pardon, both as to life and estate, merely on account of his vast and overgrown estate; so riches <hi type="italic">often take away the life of the owners thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Prov. i. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen14957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14958" type="x-p"/> 5. The more men have the more they have to lose, and perhaps they may lose it all, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.14">v. 14</reference>. Those riches that have been laid up with a great deal of pains, and kept with a great deal of care, <hi type="italic">perish by evil travail,</hi> by the very pains and care which they take to secure and increase them. Many a one has ruined his estate by being over-solicitous to advance it and make it more, and has lost all by catching at all. Riches are perishing things, and all our care about them cannot make them otherwise; they <hi type="italic">make themselves wings and fly away.</hi> He that thought he should have made his son a gentleman leaves him a beggar; he <hi type="italic">begets a son,</hi> and brings him up in the prospect of an estate, but, when he dies, leaves it under a charge of debt as much as it is worth, so that <hi type="italic">there is nothing in his hand.</hi> This is a common case; estates that made a great show do not prove what they seemed, but cheat the heir. <div eID="gen14958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14959" type="x-p"/> 6. How much soever men have when they die, they must leave it all behind them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.15-Eccl.5.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">As he came forth of his mother's womb naked, so shall he return;</hi> only as his friends, when he came naked into the world, in pity to him, helped him with swaddling-clothes, so, when he goes out, they help him with grave-clothes, and that is all. See <reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job i. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Ps. xlix. 17</reference>. This is urged as a reason why we should be content with such things as we have, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.7">1 Tim. vi. 7</reference>. In respect of the body we must go as we came; the dust shall return to the earth as it was. But sad is our case if the soul return as it came, for we were born in sin, and if we die in sin, unsanctified, we had better never have been born; and that seems to be the case of the worldling here spoken of, for he is said to <hi type="italic">return in all points as he came,</hi> as sinful, as miserable, and much more so. This is a <hi type="italic">sore evil; he</hi> thinks it so whose heart is glued to the world, that he <hi type="italic">shall take nothing of his labour which he may carry away in his hand;</hi> his riches will not go with him into another world nor stand him in any stead there. If we labour in religion, the grace and comfort we get by that labour we may carry away in our hearts, and shall be the better for it to eternity; that is meat that endures. But if we labour only for the world, to fill our hands with that, we cannot take that away with us; we are born with our hands griping, but we die with them extended, letting go what we held fast. So that, upon the whole matter, he may well ask, <hi type="italic">What profit has he that has laboured for the wind?</hi> Note, Those that labour for the world labour for the wind, for that which has more sound than substance, which is uncertain, and always shifting its point, unsatisfying, and often hurtful, which we cannot hold fast, and which, if we take up with it as our portion, will no more feed us than the <hi type="italic">wind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos. xii. 1</reference>. Men will see that they have <hi type="italic">laboured for the wind</hi> when at death they find the profit of their labour is all gone, gone like the wind, they know not whither. <div eID="gen14959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14960" type="x-p"/> 7. Those that have much, if they set their hearts upon it, have not only uncomfortable deaths, but uncomfortable lives too, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">v. 17</reference>. This covetous worldling, that is so bent upon raising an estate, <hi type="italic">all his days eats in darkness and much sorrow, and it is his sickness and wrath;</hi> he has not only no pleasure of his estate, nor any enjoyment of it himself, for he <hi type="italic">eats the bread of sorrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>), but a great deal of vexation to see others eat of it. His necessary expenses make him sick, make him fret, and he seems as if he were angry that himself and those about him cannot live without meat. As we read the last clause, it intimates how ill this covetous worldling can bear the common and unavoidable calamities of human life. When he is in health he <hi type="italic">eats in darkness,</hi> always dull with care and fear about what he has; but, if he be sick, <hi type="italic">he has much sorrow and wrath with his sickness;</hi> he is vexed that his sickness takes him off from his business and hinders him in his pursuits of the world, vexed that all his wealth will not give him any ease or relief, but especially terrified with the apprehensions of death (which his diseases are the harbingers of), of leaving this world and the things of it behind him, which he has set his affections upon, and removing to a world he has made no preparation for. He has not any <hi type="italic">sorrow after a godly sort,</hi> does not <hi type="italic">sorrow to repentance,</hi> but he has <hi type="italic">sorrow and wrath,</hi> is angry at the providence of God, angry at his sickness, angry at all about him, fretful and peevish, which doubles his affliction, which a good man lessens and lightens by patience and joy in his sickness.
entries.519649faa7767dd08fbb34dfa62ca39587f5966b: <div eID="gen14960" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Enjoyment.</title> <div sID="gen14961" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Behold <hi type="italic">that</hi> which I have seen: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good and comely <hi type="italic">for one</hi> to eat and to drink, and to enjoy the good of all his labour that he taketh under the sun all the days of his life, which God giveth him: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> his portion. <hi type="super">19</hi> Every man also to whom God hath given riches and wealth, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labour; this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gift of God. <hi type="super">20</hi> For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth <hi type="italic">him</hi> in the joy of his heart. <div eID="gen14961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14962" type="x-p"/> Solomon, from the vanity of riches hoarded up, here infers that the best course we can take is to use well what we have, to serve God with it, to do good with it, and take the comfort of it to ourselves and our families; this he had pressed before, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">ch. ii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">iii. 22</reference>. Observe, 1. What it is that is here recommended to us, not to indulge the appetites of the flesh, or to take up with present pleasures or profits for our portion, but soberly and moderately to make use of what Providence has allotted for our comfortable passage through this world. We must not starve ourselves through covetousness, because we cannot afford ourselves food convenient, nor through eagerness in our worldly pursuits, nor through excessive care and grief, but <hi type="italic">eat and drink</hi> what is fit for us to keep our bodies in good plight for the serving of our souls in God's service. We must not kill ourselves with <hi type="italic">labour,</hi> and then leave others <hi type="italic">to enjoy the good</hi> of it, but take the comfort of that which our hands have laboured for, and that not now and then, but <hi type="italic">all the days of our life which God gives us.</hi> Life is God's gift, and he has appointed us <hi type="italic">the number of the days</hi> of our life (<reference osisRef="Job.14.5">Job xiv. 5</reference>); let us therefore spend those days in <hi type="italic">serving the Lord our God with joyfulness and gladness of heart.</hi> We must not do the business of our calling as a drudgery, and make ourselves slaves to it, but we must <hi type="italic">rejoice in our labour,</hi> not grasp at more business than we can go through without perplexity and disquiet, but take a pleasure in the calling wherein God has put us, and go on in the business of it with cheerfulness. This it to <hi type="italic">rejoice in our labour,</hi> whatever it is, as <hi type="italic">Zebulun in his going out and Issachar in his tents.</hi> 2. What is urged to recommend it to us. (1.) That <hi type="italic">it is good and comely</hi> to do this. It is well, and it looks well. Those that cheerfully use what God has given them thereby honour the giver, answer the intention of the gift, act rationally and generously, do good in the world, and make what they have turn to the best account, and this is both their credit and their comfort; <hi type="italic">it is good and comely;</hi> there is duty and decency in it. (2.) That it is all the good we can have out of the things of this world: <hi type="italic">It is our portion,</hi> and in doing thus we take our portion, and make the best of bad. This is our part of our worldly possession. God must have his part, the poor theirs, and our families theirs, but this is ours; it is all that falls to our lot out of them. (3.) That a heart to do thus is such a gift of God's grace as crowns all the gifts of his providence. If God has given a man <hi type="italic">riches and wealth,</hi> he completes the favour, and makes that a blessing indeed, if withal he <hi type="italic">gives him power to eat thereof,</hi> wisdom and grace to take the good of it and to do good with it. If this <hi type="italic">is God's gift,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">covet</hi> it <hi type="italic">earnestly</hi> as <hi type="italic">the best gift</hi> relating to our enjoyments in this world. (4.) That this is the way to make our own lives easy and to relieve ourselves against the many toils and troubles which our lives on earth are incident to (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall not much remember the days of his life,</hi> the days of his sorrow and sore travail, his working days, his weeping days. He shall either forget them or remember them as waters that pass away; he shall not much lay to heart his crosses, nor long retain the bitter relish of them, <hi type="italic">because God answers him in the joy of his heart,</hi> balances all the grievances of his labour with the joy of it and recompenses him for it by giving him to <hi type="italic">eat the labour of his hands.</hi> If he does not answer all his desires and expectations, in the letter of them, yet he answers them with that which is more than equivalent, <hi type="italic">in the joy of his heart.</hi> A cheerful spirit is a great blessing; it makes the yoke of our employments easy and the burden of our afflictions light.  <chapter eID="Eccl.5"/> <div eID="gen14962" type="x-p"/>

entries.1244a054035033957a1611027bed9264474fee31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8057"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1-Eccl.5.20">Ec 5:1-20</reference>.<div eID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8057"/>1. From vanity connected with kings, he passes to vanities (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ec 5:7</reference>) which may be fallen into in serving the King of kings, even by those who, convinced of the vanity of the creature, wish to worship the Creator.<div eID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Keep thy foot--</hi>In going to worship, go with considerate, circumspect, reverent feeling. The allusion is to the taking off the shoes, or sandals, in entering a temple (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Ex 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.5.15">Jos 5:15</reference>, which passages perhaps gave rise to the custom). Weiss needlessly reads, "Keep thy feast days" (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.14">Ex 23:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">17</reference>; the three great feasts).<div eID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hear--</hi>rather, "To be ready (to draw nigh with the desire) to hear (obey) is a better sacrifice than the offering of fools" [Holden]. (Vulgate; Syriac). (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">Pr 21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jr 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.21-Jer.7.23">7:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">14:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21-Amos.5.24">Am 5:21-24</reference>). The warning is against mere ceremonial self-righteousness, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Ec 7:12</reference>. Obedience is the spirit of the law's requirements (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">De 10:12</reference>). Solomon sorrowfully looks back on his own neglect of this (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.63">1Ki 8:63</reference> with <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ec 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">6</reference>). Positive precepts of God must be kept, but will not stand instead of obedience to His moral precepts. The last provided no sacrifice for wilful sin (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30">Nu 15:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">He 10:26-29</reference>). <div eID="gen12519" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b526e72476850e17836e97b736af21977686ac5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8058"/><div sID="gen12520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8058"/><hi type="bold">2. rash--</hi>opposed to the considerate reverence ("keep thy foot," <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Ec 5:1</reference>). This verse illustrates <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Ec 5:1</reference>, as to prayer in the house of God ("before God," <reference osisRef="Isa.1.12">Is 1:12</reference>); so <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.6">Ec 5:4-6</reference> as to vows. The remedy to such vanities is stated (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Ec 5:6</reference>). "Fear thou God."<div eID="gen12520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God is in heaven--</hi>Therefore He ought to be approached with carefully weighed words, by thee, a frail creature of earth. <div eID="gen12521" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8c72313bdc42390a0b61067853534edc592b9da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8059"/><div sID="gen12522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8059"/>3. As much "business," engrossing the mind, gives birth to incoherent "dreams," so many words, uttered inconsiderately in prayer, give birth to and betray "a fool's speech" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.14">Ec 10:14</reference>), [Holden and Weiss]. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ec 5:7</reference> implies that the "dream" is not a comparison, but the vain thoughts of the fool (sinner, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">Psa 73:20</reference>), arising from multiplicity of (worldly) "business." His "dream" is that God hears him for his much speaking (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.7">Mt 6:7</reference>), independently of the frame of mind [English Version and Maurer].<div eID="gen12522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fool's voice--</hi>answers to "dream" in the parallel; it comes by the many "words" flowing from the fool's "dream." <div eID="gen12523" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1162be95a08dc3c5454b0d0d3636ee2db59ca21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8060"/><div sID="gen12524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8060"/><hi type="bold">4. When thou vowest a vow unto God--</hi>Hasty words in prayer (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ec 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">3</reference>) suggest the subject of hasty vows. A vow should not be hastily made (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.35">Jud 11:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24">1Sa 14:24</reference>). When made, it must be kept (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.11">Psa 76:11</reference>), even as God keeps His word to us (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Ex 12:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.51">51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.45">Jos 21:45</reference>). <div eID="gen12524" type="x-p"/>
entries.20aa83f9c533deab1fbbb13e966bdcfde5687fd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8061"/><div sID="gen12525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8061"/>5. (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.21">De 23:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen12525" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0ba7ff0f57da7fcc4baaa367ecf6a83cdcb3d5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8062"/><div sID="gen12526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8062"/><hi type="bold">6. thy flesh--</hi>Vow not with "thy mouth" a vow (for example, fasting), which the lusts of the flesh ("body," <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Ec 2:3</reference>, Margin) may tempt thee to break (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.25">Pr 20:25</reference>).<div eID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel--</hi>the "messenger" of God (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>); minister (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Re 1:20</reference>); that is, the priest (Mal 2:7) "before" whom a breach of a vow was to be confessed (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Le 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.5">5</reference>). We, Christians, in our vows (for example, at baptism, the Lord's Supper, &c.) vow in the presence of Jesus Christ, "the angel of the covenant" (Mal 3:1), and of ministering angels as witnesses (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1Co 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>). Extenuate not any breach of them as a slight error. <div eID="gen12527" type="x-p"/>
entries.336e6fe98a032df822e8913b28a1f09a81845b81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8063"/><div sID="gen12528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8063"/>7. (See on <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">Ec 5:3</reference>). God's service, which ought to be our chief good, becomes by "dreams" (foolish fancies as of God's requirements of us in worship), and random "words," positive "vanity." The remedy is, whatever fools may do, "Fear thou God" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ec 12:13</reference>). <div eID="gen12528" type="x-p"/>
entries.e38bd5981275f7e29137ab5be5b70d0621f9a1d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8064"/><div sID="gen12529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8064"/>8. As in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>, so here the difficulty suggests itself. If God is so exact in even punishing hasty words (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1-Eccl.5.6">Ec 5:1-6</reference>), why does He allow gross injustice? In the remote "provinces," the "poor" often had to put themselves for protection from the inroads of Philistines, &c., under chieftains, who oppressed them even in Solomon's reign (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.4">1Ki 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the matter--</hi>literally, "the pleasure," or purpose (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>). Marvel not at this dispensation of God's will, as if He had abandoned the world. Nay, there is coming a capital judgment at last, and an earnest of it in partial punishments of sinners meanwhile.<div eID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">higher than the highest--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">Da 7:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">regardeth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there be higher--</hi>plural, that is, the three persons of the Godhead, or else, "regardeth not only the 'highest' kings, than whom He 'is higher,' but even the petty tyrants of the provinces, namely, the high ones who are above them" (the poor) [Weiss]. <div eID="gen12533" type="x-p"/>
entries.d768962699afd1620c1a7c2440dd8c623d5772b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8065"/><div sID="gen12534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8065"/>9. "The profit (produce) of the earth is (ordained) for (the common good of) all: even the king himself is served by (the fruits of) the field" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.10">2Ch 26:10</reference>). Therefore the common Lord of all, high and low, will punish at last those who rob the "poor" of their share in it (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pr 22:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.4-Amos.8.7">Am 8:4-7</reference>). <div eID="gen12534" type="x-p"/>
entries.45034735feb1d6c6249a9ec2e099c31f917ae33e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8066"/><div sID="gen12535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8066"/>10. Not only will God punish at last, but meanwhile the oppressive gainers of "silver" find no solid "satisfaction" in it.<div eID="gen12535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not be satisfied--</hi>so the oppressor "eateth his own flesh" (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ec 4:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ec 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with increase--</hi>is not satisfied with the gain that he makes. <div eID="gen12537" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a6b0f73411054829066aac28b9c251b3d75b7d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8067"/><div sID="gen12538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8067"/><hi type="bold">11. they ... that eat them--</hi>the rich man's dependents (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>). <div eID="gen12538" type="x-p"/>
entries.85676fd2c6efc9d60e49a9aff73748715cb97f54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8068"/><div sID="gen12539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8068"/>12. Another argument against anxiety to gain riches. "Sleep ... sweet" answers to "quietness" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.6">Ec 4:6</reference>); "not suffer ... sleep," to "vexation of spirit." Fears for his wealth, and an overloaded stomach without "laboring" (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ec 4:5</reference>), will not suffer the rich oppressor to sleep. <div eID="gen12539" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb580f897517ed8f33771bedc5c4e5a646e90271: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8069"/><div sID="gen12540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8069"/>13-14. Proofs of God's judgments even in this world (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.31">Pr 11:31</reference>). The rich oppressor's wealth provokes enemies, robbers, &c. Then, after having kept it for an expected son, he loses it beforehand by misfortune ("by evil travail"), and the son is born to be heir of poverty. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19">Ec 2:19</reference>, 23 gives another aspect of the same subject. <div eID="gen12540" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb49cf1acca51a23fd6135999d7a089714338d13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8070"/><div sID="gen12541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8070"/>16. Even supposing that he loses not his wealth before death, then at least he must go stripped of it all (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Psa 49:17</reference>).<div eID="gen12541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laboured for the wind--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">1Co 9:26</reference>). <div eID="gen12542" type="x-p"/>
entries.b087240388399d2fee24eaaa1a313cb01c942bff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8071"/><div sID="gen12543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8071"/><hi type="bold">17. eateth--</hi>appropriately put for "liveth" in general, as connected with <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ec 5:11</reference>, 12, 18.<div eID="gen12543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>opposed to "light (joy) of countenance" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ec 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pr 16:15</reference>).<div eID="gen12544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath--</hi>fretfulness, literally, "His sorrow is much, and his infirmity (of body) and wrath." <div eID="gen12545" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c9413b9d80842490bd4e5c57cdd37579de39ee9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8072"/><div sID="gen12546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8072"/>18. Returns to the sentiment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, 13, 22); translate: "Behold the good which I have seen, and which is becoming" (in a man).<div eID="gen12546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which God giveth--</hi>namely, both the good of his labor and his life.<div eID="gen12547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his portion--</hi>legitimately. It is God's gift that makes it so when regarded as such. Such a one will use, not abuse, earthly things (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">1Co 7:31</reference>). Opposed to the anxious life of the covetous (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Ec 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen12548" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d2f71249eba8a9ac247da89b361a70fe149a93d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8073"/><div sID="gen12549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8073"/>19. As <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ec 5:18</reference> refers to the "laboring" man (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Ec 5:12</reference>), so <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Ec 5:19</reference> to the "rich" man, who gets wealth not by "oppression" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Ec 5:8</reference>), but by "God's gift." He is distinguished also from the "rich" man (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ec 6:2</reference>) in having received by God's gift not only "wealth," but also "power to eat thereof," which that one has not.<div eID="gen12549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to take his portion--</hi>limits him to the lawful use of wealth, not keeping back from God His portion while enjoying his own. <div eID="gen12550" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4f989c75f8e58b700588c41fba5ff7678b50828: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8074"/><div sID="gen12551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8074"/>20. He will not remember much, looking back with disappointment, as the ungodly do (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.11">Ec 2:11</reference>), on the days of his life.<div eID="gen12551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answereth ... in the joy--</hi>God answers his prayers in giving him "power" to enjoy his blessings. Gesenius and Vulgate translate, "For God (so) occupies him with joy," &c., that he thinks not much of the shortness and sorrows of life. Holden, "Though God gives not much (as to real enjoyment), yet he remembers (with thankfulness) the days; for (he knows) God exercises him by the joy," &c. (tries him by prosperity), so Margin, but English Version is simplest. <chapter eID="Eccl.5"/>

entries.ea1d23a98ce2ee0850048029683d88c971aeb08e: <div eID="gen25439" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25440" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25441" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25441" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25440" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25442" type="x-p"/> The reverence to be observed in attending Divine worship, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.1-Ecc.5.3">Ecc 5:1-3</reference>. We should be faithful to over engagements, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.4-Ecc.5.7">Ecc 5:4-7</reference>. The oppression of the innocent, 8. The king dependent on the produce of the soil, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.9">Ecc 5:9</reference>. Against covetousness, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.10">Ecc 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>. The peace of the honest laborer, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.12">Ecc 5:12</reference>. The evil effect of riches, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.13">Ecc 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.14">Ecc 5:14</reference>. Man cannot carry his property to the grave, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.15-Ecc.5.17">Ecc 5:15-17</reference>. We should thankfully enjoy the blessings of God, <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.18-Ecc.5.20">Ecc 5:18-20</reference>. <div eID="gen25442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25443" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25444" type="x-p"/> Keep thy foot - This verse the Hebrew and all the versions join to the preceding chapter. <div eID="gen25444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25445" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having before intimated, though very briefly, that the only cure against human vanity is a due sense of religion, now enters more largely on this important subject, and gives some excellent directions with regard to the right performance of Divine service, the nature of vocal and mental prayer, the danger of rash vows, etc. - C. <div eID="gen25445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25446" type="x-p"/> The whole verse might be more literally translated thus: - "Guard thy steps as thou art going to the house of God; and approach to hearken, and not to give the sacrifice of fools, for none of them have knowledge about doing evil." "They offer gifts for their sins, and do not turn from their evil works; for they know not (they distinguish not) between good and evil." See the Chaldee.
entries.5b8a11c4d45b076f0ada9f18ed0753456b2403b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25447" type="x-p"/> Be not rash with thy mouth - Do not hasten with thy mouth; weigh thy words, feel deeply, think much, speak little. "When ye approach his altar, on your lips <div eID="gen25447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25448" type="x-p"/> Set strictest guard; and let your thoughts be pure, <div eID="gen25448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25449" type="x-p"/> Fervent, and recollected. Thus prepared, <div eID="gen25449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25450" type="x-p"/> Send up the silent breathings of your souls, <div eID="gen25450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25451" type="x-p"/> Submissive to his will." <div eID="gen25451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25452" type="x-p"/> C.
entries.55fbf192c18a62ad53fef41b65f0bb9cdff38c38: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25453" type="x-p"/> For a dream cometh - That is, as dreams are generally the effect of the business in which we have been engaged during the day; so a multitude of words evidence the feeble workings of the foolish heart.
entries.c114fe2d9c395d04e98d1238051a3ec1090b15e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25454" type="x-p"/> When thou vowest a vow - When in distress and difficulty, men are apt to promise much to God if he will relieve them; but generally forget the vow when the distress or trouble is gone by.
entries.3b71d7b312df3f181ffcf3b60b3082c376b3efd2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25455" type="x-p"/> Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, etc. - We are under constant obligations to live to God; no vow can make it more so. Yet, there may be cases in which we should bind ourselves to take up some particular cross, to perform some particular duty, to forego some particular attachment that does not tend to bring our souls nearer to God. Then, if fully determined, and strong in faith relative to the point, bind and hold fast; but if not fully, rationally, and conscientiously determined, "do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy soul to sin."
entries.e37934af788efe564550cdd747cf117b398e991e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25456" type="x-p"/> Neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error - Nor think of saying "before the cruel angel, who shall exercise authority over thee in the judgment of the great day, that thou didst it through ignorance." - Chaldee. I believe by the angel nothing else is intended than the priest, whose business it was to take cognizance of vows and offerings. See <reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Lev 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.5">Lev 5:5</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal 2:7</reference>, the priest is called the "angel of the Lord of hosts."
entries.1cdc5b7459301e3cf1fb63f6a0bcbd6df8bb2e67: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25457" type="x-p"/> In - dreams - are - divers vanities; but fear thou God - If, by the disturbed state of thy mind during the day, or by Satanic influence, thou dream of evil, do not give way to any unreasonable fears, or gloomy forebodings, of any coming mischief: - Fear God. Fear neither the dream nor its interpretation; God, will take care of and protect thee. Most certainly, he that fears God need fear nothing else. Well may an upright soul say to Satan himself, I fear God; and because I fear him, I do not fear thee.
entries.ff5e8b415c8313110e40b12047b974ca75cc022e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25458" type="x-p"/> If thou seest the oppression of the poor - For this was a frequent case under all governments; and especially in the provinces or colonies which being far from the seat of government, were generally oppressed by the sovereign's deputies. <div eID="gen25458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25459" type="x-p"/> Marvel not at the matter - החפץ hachephets, the will, i.e., of God; which permits such evils to take place; for all things shall work together for good to them that love him. "Marvel not <div eID="gen25459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25460" type="x-p"/> Ye righteous, if his dispensations here <div eID="gen25460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25461" type="x-p"/> Unequal seem. What, though disorders reign? <div eID="gen25461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25462" type="x-p"/> He still presides, and with unerring hand <div eID="gen25462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25463" type="x-p"/> Directs the vast machine. His wisdom can <div eID="gen25463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25464" type="x-p"/> From discord harmony produce; and make <div eID="gen25464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25465" type="x-p"/> Even vice itself subservient to his ends."
entries.ce4bed1f16ec3660f9fc9110d0916fb7fcd7428c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25466" type="x-p"/> The profit of the earth is for all - The earth, if properly cultivated, is capable of producing food for every living creature; and without cultivation none has a right to expect bread. <div eID="gen25466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25467" type="x-p"/> The king himself is served by the field - Without the field he cannot have supplies for his own house; and, unless agriculture flourish, the necessary expenses of the state cannot be defrayed. Thus, God joins the head and feet together; for while the peasant is protected by the king as executor of the laws, the king himself is dependent on the peasant; as the wealth of the nation is the fruit of the laborer's toil.
entries.a39b15963cb0e33b01f22c8102c80b7a4e191558: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25468" type="x-p"/> He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver - The more he gets, the more he would get; for the saying is true: - <div eID="gen25468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25469" type="x-p"/> Crescit amor nummi, quantum ipsa pecunia crescit. "The love of money increases, in proportion as money itself increases."
entries.ddba6f1408745ea6913abdeb1211fdf203fefe0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25470" type="x-p"/> When goods increase - An increase of property always brings an increase of expense, by a multitude of servants; and the owner really possesses no more, and probably enjoys much less, than he did, when every day provided its own bread, and could lay up no store for the next. But if he have more enjoyment, his cares are multiplied; and he has no kind of profit. "This also is vanity."
entries.91802c0c26249dc85f8276a08b4268e664d5fa29: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25471" type="x-p"/> The sleep of a laboring man is sweet - His labor is healthy exercise. He is without possessions, and without cares; his sleep, being undisturbed, is sound and refreshing.
entries.ab2b7902a4fea59c954a7b99975b7ad34324d10b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen25471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25472" type="x-p"/> Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt - This may be the case through various causes: <div eID="gen25472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25473" type="x-p"/> 1. He may make an improper use of them, and lose his health by them. <div eID="gen25473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25474" type="x-p"/> 2. He may join in an unfortunate partnership and lose all. <div eID="gen25474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25475" type="x-p"/> 3. His riches may excite the desire of the robber; and he may spoil him of his goods, and even take away his life. <div eID="gen25475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25476" type="x-p"/> 4. Or, he may leave them to his son, who turns profligate; spends the whole, and ruins both his body and soul. I have seen this again and again.
entries.bd51188065bdd1b12754b90fca1e3c8eb04aa400: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25477" type="x-p"/> And he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand - He has been stripped of his property by unfortunate trade or by plunderers; and he has nothing to leave to his children.
entries.81cc50ba3287c0177741497f4d216dc640ec2c90: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25478" type="x-p"/> As he came forth - However it may be, he himself shall carry nothing with him into the eternal world. If he die worth millions, those millions are dead to him for ever; so he has had no real profit from all his labors, cares, anxieties, and vast property!
entries.39c80bdd00bd6d6609bba509e50c50847ec306d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen25478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25479" type="x-p"/> All his days also he eateth in darkness - Even his enjoyments are embittered by uncertainty. He fears for his goods; the possibility of being deprived of them fills his heart with anguish. But instead of יאכל yochel, "he shall eat," ילך yelech, "he shall walk," is the reading of several MSS. He walks in darkness - he has no evidence of salvation. There is no ray of light from God to penetrate the gloom; and all beyond life is darkness impenetrable! <div eID="gen25479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25480" type="x-p"/> And wrath with his sickness - His last hours are awful; for, "Counting on long years of pleasure here, <div eID="gen25480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25481" type="x-p"/> He's quite unfurnish'd for the world to come." <div eID="gen25481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25482" type="x-p"/> Blair. <div eID="gen25482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25483" type="x-p"/> He is full of anguish at the thought of death; but the fear of it is horrible. But if he have a sense of God's wrath in his guilty conscience, what horror can be compared with his horror!
entries.4cfd7aea7d1c9e7007e6a4336bf4302aa08111bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen25483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25484" type="x-p"/> Behold that which I have seen - This is the result of my observations and experience. God gives every man, in the course of his providence, the necessaries of life; and it is his will that he should thankfully use them. <div eID="gen25484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25485" type="x-p"/> For it is his portion - What is requisite for him in the lower world; without them his life cannot subsist, and earthly blessings are as truly the portion of his body and animal life, as the salvation of God is the portion of his soul.
entries.2aa85f9e8f3fb7ef5f6186f23bac1feb33780499: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen25485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25486" type="x-p"/> For he shall not much remember - The person who acts in this way, extracts all the good requisite from life.
